aspects.title: CSS-reordered visual layout makes DOM/tab order contradict the meaningful order (no tabindex, no script)
aspects.description: A page uses NO positive tabindex and NO focus-managing script, so every static 'tabindex misuse' heuristic finds nothing. But CSS (flexbox `order`, grid placement, float, absolute positioning) reorders the visual presentation so that the natural DOM tab order no longer follows the meaning conveyed by the rendered layout. G59's core point applies: 'When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.' Judging a violation requires looking at the RENDERED page, inferring the intended reading/operation sequence from the visual hierarchy, and comparing it to the keyboard sequence. The Understanding makes this an explicit judgment: independent columns out of order do NOT fail, but interdependent content out of order DOES. This is the most semantically demanding limb and the highest-value uncovered space.
aspects.scLimb: Focus-order-vs-reading-order independence limb / core meaning limb: 'Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout... as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved.'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT rules/cases for 2.4.3. F44 (the only automatable-adjacent failure) is scoped to the tabindex attribute; a page with zero tabindex and zero script presents nothing for a static rule to inspect. No automated tool can decide whether visually-reordered DOM content is 'independent' (passes) or 'interdependent' (fails) — that is the exact distinction the Understanding flags as requiring human consideration of the rendered presentation.

references.quote: When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.

if the two columns are independent of each other, and meaning/operation are not affected, it is not a failure if elements in the right-hand column receive focus first, followed by the elements in the left-hand column.

Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout of the web page, as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages where CSS (flex `order`, grid `grid-row/column`, float, absolute positioning) detaches visual order from DOM/tab order, with NO tabindex and NO JS. Capture a screenshot of the rendered page AND derive the keyboard tab sequence; the failing/passing verdict turns on whether the DOM-order sequence preserves the meaning implied by the visual layout. Always pair an interdependent FAIL variant with an independent PASS variant (e.g. the Understanding's two-column independent case, and the 'nav after main in source, CSS to the left' passing example) so a judge is measured on both over-flagging and under-flagging.
suggestedScenarios: Checkout page where CSS flex `order` visually places 'Place order' at the bottom but its DOM position makes it the FIRST tab stop, so keyboard focus reaches submit before quantity/address — meaning broken, no tabindex (FAIL).
Two-column plan-comparison form where the DOM interleaves the columns so tab goes Basic-name, Pro-name, Basic-email, Pro-email; the columns are interdependent comparison rows (FAIL).

Independent two-column layout (e.g. a 'main article' column and an unrelated 'newsletter signup' column) where CSS puts the signup visually right but it tabs first — meaning/operation unaffected (PASS, must NOT be flagged).
Passing source-order trick from the Understanding: left-hand nav placed AFTER main content in the HTML, CSS-positioned to the left, so main content tabs first without tabindex (PASS).
Multi-step wizard rendered with CSS grid where step 3's controls precede step 1's controls in the DOM, so focus jumps to a later step before the earlier one (FAIL).
A form whose label/input pairs are visually stacked correctly but CSS `order` swaps two fields so 'Confirm password' tabs before 'Password' (FAIL).
Pricing cards where flex `order` reverses the visual sequence (cheapest-to-priciest visually) while DOM keeps original order, so tab traverses prices opposite to the implied layout direction (FAIL).

aspects.title: Focus order interleaves between two semantically distinct sections/groups (the canonical Understanding form failure)
aspects.description: The Understanding's own failing example: a form has a mailing/marketing-data section (name, address, city, state, postal) and a separate newsletter-checkbox section, but the tab order jumps between sections — name, then a checkbox, then street address, then another checkbox. Every field has a correct visible label, correct programmatic name/role, and is fully keyboard-operable; the interleaving can be produced purely by DOM order with no tabindex for a tool to flag. The failure is visible ONLY to an evaluator who understands which fields 'belong together' semantically (mailing-address fields form one group; newsletter choices form another) and that crossing between groups mid-sequence destroys the user's mental model. G59's applicant/spouse example is the passing mirror.
aspects.scLimb: Core meaning limb: 'focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning'. Concretely the Understanding's failing example of tab order skipping between distinct form sections.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. The fields are individually valid (labels present, operable), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing — they have no model of which fields belong together semantically. Deciding that 'street address' belongs with 'city/state/postal' and NOT between two newsletter checkboxes is pure content-meaning grouping, exactly what the SC leaves to human judgment.

references.quote: the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox.
All the interactive elements in the applicant section receive focus before any of the elements in the spouse section. The elements in each section receive focus in the reading order of that section.
Determine if the focus order impacts the page meaning (e.g., form fields for a mailing address are presented in the expected sequence).

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build forms with two (or more) visually-grouped sections under clear headings. Produce the interleaving via raw DOM ordering (no tabindex) so each field is individually valid. Verify the actual Tab sequence zig-zags across group boundaries. Pair each FAIL with the G59 passing counter-example (all of group A tabbed before any of group B) using near-identical markup so a judge cannot pass by simply detecting 'two groups exist'.
suggestedScenarios: Registration form with 'Billing address' (4 fields) and 'Shipping address' (4 fields) as two visual boxes, but tab order alternates billing-line1, shipping-line1, billing-line2, shipping-line2 (FAIL).
Survey with a 'Demographics' group and a 'Preferences' group whose controls interleave so the user answers age, favorite-color, gender, favorite-food in a confusing weave (FAIL).
Booking form where outbound-flight fields and return-flight fields alternate in tab order although visually grouped under two headings (FAIL).
Contact form where name/email/message are correctly grouped but a 'how did you hear about us' checkbox set is spliced into the middle so tab goes name, checkbox, email, checkbox, message (FAIL).
Passing counter-example: an applicant/co-applicant loan form where all applicant fields are tabbed before any co-applicant field (G59 pattern) — must NOT be flagged (PASS).
Job application with 'Education' and 'Work experience' sections where tab order zig-zags between an education row and an experience row (FAIL).

aspects.title: Revealed non-modal dialog/menu is not next in the navigation order (F85, open branch)
aspects.description: F85's core failure: a trigger button reveals an in-page dialog or menu, but the revealed widget is NOT focus-managed AND is not next in the sequential navigation order — typically because the dialog markup sits at the end of the DOM. After activating the trigger, the keyboard user's focus stays on (or just after) the trigger, so to reach the visually-overlaid dialog they must tab through the entire rest of the page. On a self-contained HTML page this is testable with a tiny script that only toggles visibility (no focus move). It requires multi-state interaction judgment: you must activate the control, then evaluate where focus lands relative to where it visually/logically should be. This is the TT 4.F step 2b 'reveal hidden content... check the focus order to, from, and within the revealed content' manual step.
aspects.scLimb: Revealed/hidden-content traversal limb (TT 4.F step 2b) + F85 open branch — focus to/within revealed content not adjacent to its trigger.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 2.4.3, and F85 is explicitly a manual procedure ('Activate the trigger control via the keyboard'). Static analysis cannot know that the visually-overlaid dialog is the user's intended next interaction; it sees a hidden div somewhere in the DOM. No automated tool simulates 'open, then check the next Tab stop is in the dialog.'

references.quote: If focus is not set to the dialog or menu, or a logical focusable descendent of these widgets, and the widget or a focusable descendent is not next in the sequential navigation order, it will be difficult for the keyboard user to operate the dialog or menu.

Since the dialog is found at the end of the DOM, it is at the end of the keyboard navigation order. Because a user's focus isn't managed... the user will need to tab through the rest of the web page before they can interact with the dialog.

It may be necessary to use the keyboard to activate trigger controls that reveal hidden content with focusable elements (menus, dialogs, modal dialog boxes, expandable tree list) to check the focus order to, from, and within the revealed content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single-page HTML with a trigger button near the top and the revealed widget markup at the END of the DOM. Script only toggles visibility/display (NO focus move). The verdict requires activating the trigger and inspecting whether the very next Tab stop is inside the widget. Pair with the Understanding's non-modal PASS example (widget markup placed immediately after the trigger so it IS next in tab order, no focus script needed).
suggestedScenarios: 'Subscribe' button near the top opens a newsletter dialog whose markup is the last element before </body>; focus stays on the button so Tab walks all page links first (FAIL).
Nav 'Menu' button reveals a flyout placed at end of DOM with no focus move, so Tab from the button goes to page content, not the menu items (FAIL).
PASS counter-example (Understanding non-modal): same subscribe dialog but markup placed immediately after the trigger so it is next in tab order, no focus script (PASS).
'Filter' button opens an inline filter panel positioned at the bottom of the DOM; visually beside the button but tab order requires traversing the whole results list to reach it (FAIL).
'Reply' button under a comment reveals a reply form appended at the very end of the comment-thread DOM, so focus does not advance into the just-opened form (FAIL).
Help '?' icon reveals a tooltip-dialog with a focusable 'Got it' button rendered at end of DOM — Tab after the icon does not reach it (FAIL).

aspects.title: Focus not returned (or returned illogically) after a dialog/menu is dismissed (F85, close branch + modal return)
aspects.description: F85's second failure branch and the Understanding's modal example: after the user dismisses an in-page menu or dialog, focus is dumped on document.body (or scrolls to top), forcing the user to tab from the very start of the page back to where they were. The pass condition is nuanced: focus should return to the trigger control, OR — if the trigger was removed by the action — to a logical neighboring element (F85's tag-delete note). Evaluating this requires understanding what the 'logical' return point is given what the action did: deleting an item should move focus to the next item, not the top of the page; cancelling should return to the trigger. This is a state-transition reasoning task.
aspects.scLimb: Revealed/hidden-content traversal limb (focus FROM revealed content, TT 4.F step 2b) + F85 close branch + Understanding modal 'focus returns to the button or the element following the button'.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. The 'where should focus go after close' decision depends on the semantics of the action that closed the widget (cancel vs delete vs save), which no static tool models. F85 marks it manual ('Check whether keyboard focus is put back on the trigger control'). The 'logical neighbor' exception means even a tool that naively checked 'focus == trigger' would mis-fire on the legitimate delete-then-move-to-next case.

references.quote: When a menu is dismissed, it is removed or hidden from the web page and focus is set to the document. The user must tab from the beginning of the navigation sequence to reach the point from which the menu was opened.

If the trigger control itself was removed as a result of the activation, check if the focus has been put on the interactive element immediately preceding or following the removed trigger control, or wherever is logical.
When the dialog is dismissed, focus returns to the button or the element following the button.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Single-page HTML with a trigger that opens a widget and a close/confirm/cancel control. Script the dismissal to set focus either to document.body / top (FAIL) or to the trigger / a logical neighbor (PASS). Include the F85 tag-delete PASS case where the trigger is removed and focus correctly moves to the next list item (must NOT be flagged). The verdict requires opening, dismissing, then checking where focus landed relative to the action semantics.
suggestedScenarios: Settings dialog whose Close button hides the dialog and sets focus to document.body, dropping the user to the top of the page (FAIL).
Delete-confirmation modal where, after confirming, focus is sent to the top of the page rather than the next list item (FAIL).
PASS case (F85 note): a tag list where deleting a tag closes the dialog and focus moves to the NEXT tag in the list — does not return to the now-removed trigger but is logical (PASS).
Escape-key dismissal of a search overlay that leaves focus on the now-hidden (aria-hidden) overlay container, so the next Tab starts from page top (FAIL).
PASS counter-example: a menu closed by clicking a menu item returns focus to the trigger button (PASS) — paired with a near-identical variant that resets focus to body (FAIL).
Multi-step modal whose final 'Done' button closes it and correctly returns focus to the originating 'Edit profile' button (PASS).

aspects.title: Modal dialog focus is not contained — forward Tab or backward Shift+Tab escapes behind the inert backdrop
aspects.description: The Understanding modal example and TT 4.F step 3 require that for a modal, keyboard focus navigating BOTH forward and backward remains within the dialog until it closes, with outside content inert. The subtle, human-judgment failure: a 'modal' that looks modal (dim backdrop, centered card) and may even trap forward Tab, but Shift+Tab (backward) escapes to the page behind it, or the last element's forward Tab leaks to page content. Because TT says backward order need not mirror forward but must still preserve operability, evaluating containment requires testing BOTH directions and judging whether escaped focus lands the user somewhere that destroys the modal's operability. This is distinct from a 2.1.2 keyboard trap (inability to leave); here the failure is leaving when the user should be contained.
aspects.scLimb: Modal-dialog containment limb (TT 4.F step 3: 'keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed') + backward-focus-order limb (TT 4.F step 2d).
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. Containment is a runtime, bidirectional interaction property: a static rule cannot determine that a div with role=dialog actually keeps focus inside under Shift+Tab, nor that the backdrop content was made inert. The forward-vs-backward asymmetry (forward trapped, backward leaking) is precisely the manual both-directions check TT calls out and no automated checker performs.

references.quote: For modal dialog boxes, keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed.
As long as the dialog is open, all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus
Backward focus order does not have to mirror the forward focus order. However, it must preserve the meaning and operability of the page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build a visually-modal dialog (backdrop + centered card) with focusable controls and minimal JS. Create variants: (a) forward Tab trapped but Shift+Tab leaks to the page behind (FAIL); (b) last-element forward Tab leaks to page content (FAIL); (c) fully-contained both directions with outside content inert (PASS). The verdict requires driving BOTH Tab and Shift+Tab and observing whether focus ever lands outside the dialog while open. Keep clearly distinct from 2.1.2 (do not build a trap that cannot be exited at all).
suggestedScenarios: Modal that traps forward Tab (cycles last->first) but Shift+Tab from the first control escapes to the page header behind the backdrop (FAIL).
Modal where forward Tab from the last control leaks to a page link behind the dialog instead of cycling to the first control (FAIL).
Fully-contained modal: both Tab and Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog and outside content is inert/aria-hidden (PASS).
Modal that visually dims the page but never set the background inert, so Tab silently walks onto background form fields the user cannot see has focus (FAIL).
Modal whose containment works forward but a stray focusable element (a skip-link) outside the dialog still receives Shift+Tab focus (FAIL).
PASS counter-example with intentionally different backward order inside the dialog (Shift+Tab visits controls in a non-mirrored but still-operable order) — must NOT be flagged (PASS).

aspects.title: Multiple valid orders — row-wise vs column-wise grid/table traversal must NOT be flagged
aspects.description: The false-positive trap built into the SC: when content has two-dimensional structure (a table of interactive controls, a grid of cards), EITHER row-by-row OR column-by-column focus order can satisfy the SC because both 'reflect the logical relationships in the content.' An evaluator must recognize that a column-wise tab order through a data-entry table is NOT a violation just because it isn't the more common row-wise order — provided meaning/operation are preserved. The hard judgment is distinguishing 'a different-but-valid logical order' from 'an order that destroys meaning.' The SC explicitly says only one valid order need be provided. This aspect exists to measure whether a judge OVER-flags valid alternatives.
aspects.scLimb: Multiple-valid-orders limb: 'There may be different orders that reflect logical relationships... Either order may satisfy this success criterion' and 'If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided.'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. An automated tool has no concept of 'this alternative order still reflects a logical relationship'; it would either ignore order entirely or naively flag any non-source/non-left-to-right order. The spec demands the evaluator simultaneously hold several acceptable orders — a reasoning task, not a pattern match.

references.quote: moving through components in a table one row at a time or one column at a time both reflect the logical relationships in the content. Either order may satisfy this success criterion.
If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided.
Focus order does not necessarily need to be top to bottom, left to right.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build 2-D grids/tables of interactive controls and drive the tab order column-major (where the source default would be row-major) using DOM ordering. The correct verdict for a legitimate column-wise workflow is PASS. Each PASS scenario should be paired with a near-identical FAIL where the order snakes randomly/diagonally with no logical relationship, so the judge is measured on telling 'valid alternative' from 'meaning-destroying' rather than blindly flagging any non-row-major order.
suggestedScenarios: 3x3 product-matrix of quantity inputs where tab moves column-by-column (down each column then across) — logical (PASS).
Weekly timetable of checkboxes (rows=time slots, columns=days) tabbed day-by-day vertically; meaning preserved (PASS).
Budget-entry spreadsheet (columns=months, rows=categories) where column-wise tab (enter all of January first) is a legitimate workflow (PASS).
Matrix rating question (rows=statements, columns=agree/neutral/disagree) tabbed column-major; still meaningful (PASS).
Seating-chart picker tabbed row-wise across seats (PASS) — paired with a near-identical one whose tab order snakes diagonally with no relationship (FAIL).
Calendar widget where tab order goes week-by-week down then across (column orientation) — valid alternative (PASS) — vs one that scatters cells randomly (FAIL).

aspects.title: Confusing/illogical focus stops from nested focusable wrappers or focusable static content
aspects.description:
The Understanding note: the SC 'does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable,' BUT 'it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements' (e.g. `
`). The judgment is whether the extra/duplicate/odd focus stops impede meaning or operability: a control that appears to receive focus twice, a tabindex=0 on a non-interactive wrapper that injects a meaningless stop mid-sequence, or static text that grabs focus between two related controls and breaks the flow. Whether such stops merely add tedium (best-practice, not a failure) or actually 'impede meaning/operation' (a failure) is exactly the human line the note draws.
aspects.scLimb: Static/non-interactive-focusable + nested-focusable limb (Understanding note): non-operable focusable content is allowed unless it 'impedes meaning/operation' or creates 'confusing or illogical focus orders... a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. A tool can mechanically count tabindex=0 attributes but cannot judge whether a focus stop is 'confusing or illogical' or whether a double-focus (wrapper + child) 'impedes meaning'. The note explicitly permits focusable static content; only the meaning-impeding subset fails, which is a contextual human judgment, not a static pattern.

references.quote: it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.
This success criterion does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable, or programmatically moving focus to such content.
Static/non-interactive elements can receive focus, as long as they don't impede operation of the content, or result in confusing or illogical focus order.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with focusable static/wrapper elements and inspect the resulting tab sequence. FAIL variants: a div[tabindex=0] wrapping a button so the same control appears to receive focus twice; a tabindex=0 paragraph injected between a label and its input breaking the flow; static text stops scattered through a form. PASS variants: focusable static content placed where it does NOT impede meaning (e.g. a focusable status message at a logical point), to test the judge does not flag every focusable non-interactive element. The verdict turns on 'impedes meaning/operation' vs merely 'tedious'.

aspects.title: Positive tabindex creates a tab order that does not preserve meaning (F44), with the meaning-judgment a human must make
aspects.description: F44: positive tabindex values impose an explicit tab order that does not follow the content's logical relationships and sequences (the <ol> example tabbing Homepage, chapter 3, chapter 2, chapter 1). While a static tool can DETECT the presence of positive tabindex (axe flags it as best-practice), the actual 2.4.3 failure requires judging that the resulting order breaks meaning — a positive-tabindex page whose order happens to match the content sequence is NOT a failure, and a positive tabindex that re-establishes the correct order after a CSS reflow can even be the fix. So the human contribution is deciding whether the imposed numeric order preserves or destroys meaning/operability, and recognizing the common edit-drift case (a new field without tabindex gets pushed to the end).
aspects.scLimb: tabindex-misuse failure (F44): positive tabindex creating a tab order that does not follow content sequence/relationships.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT rules cover F44. Automated tools can surface 'positive tabindex present' as a best-practice warning but cannot decide whether the specific numeric order preserves or breaks meaning — they would either flag every positive tabindex (false positives on correctly-ordered ones, and on the legitimate 'tabindex used to repair CSS reflow' case) or none. The meaning-preservation judgment is human; that is why this is kept but at lower priority than the no-tabindex aspects.

Detecting the doubled stop requires tabbing the grid, noticing each story is reached twice, and judging the nested-focusable duplication confusing. Verified live: tab order alternates card -> 'Read more' -> card -> 'Read more' (8 stops for 4 destinations).

None material. This is an intentional inapplicable/boundary (negative) case: there is no accessibility error by design, which matches the documented expected outcome of 'inapplicable'. errorIsReal=false reflects the absence of a defect (as intended), not a flaw in the case.

None that undermine the case. One adversarial nuance: this sits at the soft/judgment-heavy end of 2.4.3 — every field is independently completable, so operability is technically preserved; the 'failure' rests on meaning/flow being broken by interleaving two distinct sections. This is defensible because it faithfully reproduces the SC's own normative failing example, but it is not a hard trap or programmatic-order violation, so a strict reviewer could debate the binary 'failed' label. This ambiguity is precisely what makes it appropriate for a human-judgment corpus rather than a defect.

No defect: this is a deliberate G59 PASS counter-example. There is no claimed accessibility error to confirm — errorIsReal=false reflects 'no issue exists', which is consistent with the documented outcome of 'passed'. The page is correct, not broken.

Minor labeling note: the .md 'Element / selector carrying the issue' header is slightly misleading since there is no issue; it does clarify in body text that #c-name is inspected to show it receives focus only after the last applicant field. Not a substantive problem.

Minor (not disqualifying): SC 2.4.3 carries an inherent interpretive ambiguity here. A row-wise sequence (name,name -> email,email ...) could in principle be argued as a valid 'compare two attendees row by row' order. The page resolves this in favor of 'failed' because the visual presentation is two separate headed/bordered cards (form::before right card = Attendee 1, form::after left card = Attendee 2), not a shared comparison table, so the per-attendee grouping is the conveyed meaning and the interleave breaks it. Folder-level (not unique to case-06): all six cases share the same 'interleaved-focus-between-semantic-groups' grid-areas re-routing mechanism. case-06's content domain (job-board/ATS CV form, single-column stacked Education-over-Work) is meaningfully distinct from the five siblings (e-commerce, nonprofit, travel, banking, events), so it is not a duplicate, but reviewers should ensure the corpus is not over-weighted toward this single CSS-grid-reorder pattern.
No defect — this is an intentional PASS counter-example and the 'passed' label is correct. There is no accessibility issue (errorIsReal=false is the EXPECTED state for this case, not a defect).

Minor doc nuance: the .md says case-01/02 'both contain a role=dialog' identical to case-03; siblings differ slightly in trigger/markup, but the static-indistinguishability claim that matters (axe/WAVE return no issues on both pass and fail) holds and was confirmed empirically. Not blocking.

DOC NARRATIVE GEOMETRICALLY WRONG (not an outcome error): the .md repeatedly claims the panel 'appears visually right under the button' / 'right beside the button on the left' and that magnifier users 'see the filter controls beside the button.' In reality the toolbar h1 has flex:1, pushing both buttons to the FAR RIGHT (button x=938 at 1280px, x=526 at 768px), while the panel is pinned FAR LEFT (position:fixed; left:26px; x=26), separated by ~800-912px on desktop and overlapping the first results column. The page's own .md body correctly acknowledges this ('no role="menu"'). Selector ambiguity: the orchestrator's 'Element under test' is #exploreMega (the panel), while the .md frames the defect as the trigger/panel PAIR (#exploreBtn + #exploreMega). The pair is the correct unit for an F85 focus-order failure; neither element alone is the whole defect. Not a correctness problem, just imprecise scoping.

The trigger does advertise aria-haspopup='true' + aria-controls, so treating the revealed form as a popup widget is a defensible functional extension of F85 — the SC 2.4.3 violation is genuine — but it is not a literal role=dialog case.

Note (not a defect): the static inspect tool reports the closed-form tab order (form is display:none, so its controls are absent and the order ends at footer stop 16). The failure only manifests after opening the form; this was confirmed with a dynamic puppeteer probe rather than the static tool snapshot.

Mechanism narration is imprecise (not verdict-breaking): the prompt's 'Claimed mechanism' asserts that after Escape 'activeElement is #q with a 0x0 box inside a display:none container.' My Puppeteer probe contradicts this — applying display:none (closeSearch removes the .open class) causes Chromium to auto-blur the hidden #q input and revert activeElement to document.body (afterEsc.activeId = 'BODY', activeIsBody = true, activeInsideHiddenOverlay = false). Focus is NOT stranded on #q; it falls back to the document. The .md doc itself is more accurate on this point (line 36: 'falls back toward the document/body') though it also carries a loose clause ('focus is left on a hidden node'). Recommend tightening the wording so it does not claim focus remains on #q.

No defect in the verdict: F85 Tests step 2 ('Check whether keyboard focus is put back on the trigger control') is FALSE for both the Escape and Close-button paths (focus = body, not #open-search), and the trigger was not removed, so the second sub-check is inapplicable/false — by F85 Expected Results 'both points under step 2 false' the page fails SC 2.4.3. The body/document fallback exactly matches the cited F85 example ('focus is set to the document. The user must tab from the beginning of the navigation sequence...').

Minor (tool artifact, not a page defect): the inspect.js `tabOrder` field shows a clean modal-only cycle (amt/when/cancel/confirm repeated) and never surfaces the Log-out leak, because it is a static DOM-focusable walker, not a real key-event simulation. The actual leak is only visible when real Shift+Tab key events are dispatched (which I did via Puppeteer).

Minor: the .md cites TWO references; the second (Understanding 2.4.3 inert example) is paraphrased by trimming the parenthetical, but the load-bearing clause 'all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus' is verbatim and correctly attributed. No defect.

Minor (non-defect): the element-under-test selector #promo is just the anchor section; the actual failure is the ABSENCE of containment plus the still-focusable background controls (#q/#q-go). Consistent with the doc, which names #promo/#scrim as the pseudo-modal and #q/#q-go as leak targets, so not an error.

Focus still leaves the modal backward and reaches the banner, so the both-direction-leak verdict holds, but the doc's 'directly onto those same buttons' phrasing overstates the precise key sequence. Consider tightening the wording.

The exact-mechanism section's stated forward cycle '#card -> #cycle -> #cancel -> #pay -> #cookie-accept -> #cookie-manage -> (wrap to #card)' omits the intervening body/document-boundary stop that Chromium inserts on wrap (inspect tabOrder stop 5 = 'body/none'); cosmetic only.

Doc/HTML claim '0 page-content focus hits over 20 Tabs' is technically inaccurate: at the native-<dialog> focus-wrap boundary document.activeElement becomes BODY (tabIndex -1), 2 such hits per 20 presses each direction. It is a Chromium wrap artifact (no operable background control is ever reachable), so the PASS is unaffected, but the evidence wording overstates and should read 'no operable page content reached in either direction'.

None material. This is a PASS/false-positive-trap case (documented Failure mechanism: NONE), so errorIsReal=false is the INTENDED state, not a defect: no genuine 2.4.3 violation exists, which is exactly what the page is designed to demonstrate. Minor nomenclature: the verbatim citation grep failed on a single line only because both reference files line-wrap the quoted sentences; after whitespace normalization BOTH quotes are present character-for-character (focus-order.html line ~97; F44.html line ~7). Not a real citation defect.

Secondary citation in case-05.md references 'wcag-understanding/focus-order.html', which does not exist anywhere under refs/ (find returned only the trusted-tester file). The quoted WCAG-Understanding sentence cannot be verified against the corpus. This is a minor documentation defect; it does not affect the verdict because the prompt's authoritative citation (refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.3-focus-order.md) is verified verbatim.

A focusable-interactive-inside-focusable-interactive with identical accessible name is a recognizable anti-pattern a heuristic checker could flag, even though no mainstream axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule does so today. requiresHumanJudgment still holds because judging the duplicate stop as 'confusing' vs 'harmlessly tedious' is a semantic call, but this nuance should be acknowledged.

Severity is genuinely low: both stops activate the same working control (wrapper keydown re-dispatches the inner button's click), so nothing is blocked — the harm is ambiguity/cognitive confusion (the mildest end of 'impedes operation'), not loss of access.

Citation note caveat: the quoted sentence ('a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements') plus the <div tabindex=0><button> example matches the LOCAL vendored wcag-understanding/focus-order.html lines 79-81 verbatim, and the .md correctly attributes it to that file. Reviewers relying on pristine upstream W3C text should note this note paragraph appears to be an augmented/vendored addition; against the named local reference it is exact and correct.

G59 secondary citation is a weaker fit: G59 governs the ordering of INTERACTIVE elements in a sequence, whereas the defect here is a NON-interactive element wedged into the tab order. It is still tangentially relevant (sequential fields) and is verbatim, but the primary focus-order.html 'For clarity' citation is the authoritative one and is exactly on point.

Scenario narrative cites a 'reveal-on-focus / scroll-reveal animation' as the motivation for tabindex=0, but no JS implementing any such animation exists in the page (jsErrors:[], no script). This does not weaken the focus-order defect (which is fully present from the tabindex alone) but the stated motivation is narrative-only.

This is a genuine borderline-judgment SC: whether a single meaningless mid-sequence focus stop rises to a 2.4.3 FAILURE vs a harmless-but-suboptimal stop is contestable. The 'failed' label is defensible given the stop sits inside a tightly-coupled card-entry chain, but a reviewer could argue 'cantTell'. This contestability is exactly what makes it a human-judgment case (a plus for the corpus), not a defect.

Browser tab order confirms consecutive double stops per timed step: stop0 span named '2 Sear ... Start 30 min timer', stop1 button 'Start 30 min timer' (and analogously steps 3 & 4). The span IS in the focus order and receives focus (outline applied); the tabOrder 'name' field flattens its descendant text to '2 Sear ... Start 30 min timer', so the perceived AT double-stop is genuine. Does not undermine the failure.
The prompt's own quoted citation sentence is the wrong half for this page (it belongs to the mismatched remittance scenario), but the MD doc's two citations are correct and verbatim.

MECHANISM ABSENT: The cited 2.4.3 failure is 'a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to NESTED focusable elements' — the note illustrates this with <div tabindex=0><button>. The actual page has NO nesting: the two links per card (a.cover and a.listen) are SIBLINGS, both direct children of li.episode (AX tree: parent_role=listitem for all 8 links). The page has zero tabindex and zero role attributes (doc admits 'No role attribute is present anywhere'). The nested-focusable structure the citation requires does not exist.

STOPS ARE DISTINGUISHABLE (doc claim is false): The doc says the two stops are 'indistinguishable', but the AX tree gives them clearly different accessible names: cover link = 'Episode 142: The night the harbor lights went out', second = 'Listen now ▸'. An AT user does NOT perceive 'the same control twice.'

NOT A 2.4.3 FAILURE: Focus order follows DOM/visual reading order exactly (title-link → its Listen-link → next card). 2.4.3 governs the ORDER of focus, not the COUNT of stops. Nothing impedes meaning or operation; the order is logical. The real (minor) pattern is redundant/duplicate links to one destination, which is a 2.4.4/redundancy concern at most and is generally considered conforming.
